svg.text: SANDBOX A: own view, filter, limits
SANDBOX B: same build, shares nothing
TB3 · EXISTS — connections via the mediator
(l) builds the sandbox before any integration
code runs, with its own channel, so the
identity is fixed before the code starts
the platform it gets is local and empty
exactly the grant shown, in Repairs,
or the operator at the device
6 of 6 boundaries enforced — in Figure 8.1, four of the six were absent
EXISTS — this design puts an enforcement point here; in Figure 8.1 there was none
UNCHANGED / NARROWED — existed in Figure 8.1; TB4 is as it was, TB2 is narrowed
(b′) · (c′) · (d′) · (h′) — a primed flow replaces the same-letter flow of Figure 8.1; (l) to (o) are new
Compare with Figure 8.1. Five flows drawn there are absent here: (e) the shared memory, (f) reading any integration's stored credentials, (g) reading any file,
(i) reaching another integration's objects and (j) home network access. None of the five is refused by a check. The stored settings and the secrets file are not in the
sandbox's view, the two integrations are separate processes, and addresses in the home are refused by default, so there is no request to make.
TB5 and TB6 are crossed by no flow at all, and that is deliberate rather than an omission: in Figure 8.1 those same two places carried (e), (f), (g), (i) and (j). A boundary nothing crosses is the
strongest form this design produces, because nothing has to decide correctly for it to hold.
TB2 is narrowed, not closed. The mediator connects as an ordinary Home Assistant user that the bridge designates, so it can no longer create users, change the configuration or install integrations,
but it can still operate every device, because the platform cannot limit a user to some devices through a supported interface. That is residual risk R3, High, narrowed. Flow (m) is new:
no grant reaches a sandbox until a person has approved exactly what was shown.
